newsitem.title: UK: UK could learn from Australian jobs scheme - report.
newsitem.headline: UK could learn from Australian jobs scheme - report.

text.p: Britain's Labour government's proposed "welfare-to-work" jobs programme would benefit by learning lessons from similar Australian schemes, a conference heard on Monday.

"Many of the ideas considered by Britain's new government bear a striking similarity to initiatives which were tried in Australia," said Paul Convery, director of the Unemployment Unit, a pressure group.
"There are many valuable and innovative ideas which may be applicable to Britain and there may be some cautionary lessons to be learnt too."
By levying a "windfall tax" on Britain's privatised utilities, Labour plans to spend 3.0 billion pounds ($4.9 billion) to create jobs for 250,000 young and long-term unemployed.
The conference was attended by education and employment minister Alan Howarth, who said he welcomed the chance to learn from Australia's experience before Labour implemented its own reforms.
"We don't have all the answers and that's why consultation with you is so important," he said.
Dr Dan Finn of the Unemployment Unit, who studied the "Working Nation" programme in Australia, said it had stumbled because many employers failed to take up the subsidies on offer.

Australia aimed to reduce its long-term unemployed by injecting A$6.3 ($4.9) billion over three years into a "job compact" subsidy scheme which guaranteed employment to anyone out of work for more than 18 months.
Labour has said its programme will be "comfortably" funded by the windfall tax. It too will offer employers subsidies to take unemployed people on.

The Australian jobs programme sought to improve labour market efficiency by increasing awareness among the unemployed -- explaining what areas of work were open to them and targeting jobs to apply for.
But the net effect of the scheme did not create more jobs, although it did boost the chances of long-term jobless people finding work, Finn said.
Despite reducing the number of long-term unemployed by 20 percent in the first 18 months, "Working Nation" was undermined by the failure of many employers to respond to the job subsidies available.

Many employers were reluctant to take on people they saw as undesirable employees, said Finn, while in their efforts to hit government targets to reduce the unemployment rate, administrators pushed people into community jobs which did work-seekers little good, he added.
Howarth agreed that creating jobs for the sake of it would be short sighted.
"Employers have got to be very positively disposed and committed," Howarth said. "We are at great risk of simply churning people around without having any net new jobs."
Finn said supply-side measures, which aim to boost production through tax cuts, could help the long-term unemployed compete for jobs.
"But it is sustained employment growth that is the key to reducing the number of people dependent on the benefit system," Finn said.

Howarth said:"If we are to do anything at all to help people escape from the poverty trap then we are going to need the minimum wage, we are going to need the 10 pence starting (rate of income) tax and we are going to need reforms to the benefits system".
In keeping with Australia's programme, he said the government would have to intervene to boost workers' skills to encourage blue-chip employers to take on the unemployed.

"Even if we can remove the mathematical and technical problems which stop people escaping from the poverty trap, they have got to have skills, they've got to have self-confidence to be able to seize those opportunities." ($ = 0.610 British Pounds) ($ = 1.291 Australian Dollars)
